Hey there! Welcome to the Sparrow Sync docs! 🐦

Sparrow Sync is a Paper and Folia plugin for synchronizing player data across Minecraft servers. It coordinates player sessions through Redis and stores player data as persistent snapshots, so players keep their progress when they move between servers — and administrators can recover earlier saves at any time. info Sparrow Sync captures player state on the appropriate server thread (fully Folia-compatible), then encodes and stores snapshots asynchronously. Tasks for the same player are always processed in order, so a busy network never writes data out of sequence.

Inventories, ender chests, experience, health, hunger, potion effects, advancements, statistics, attributes, location and more — every data type can be toggled individually in the configuration. Map data can also be shared between servers, with configurable synchronization modes and interaction controls.

🗄️ Flexible storage — MongoDB, MySQL or PostgreSQL for persistence, with Redis handling cross-server coordination 📦 Compressed snapshots — player data stored with Sparrow NBT, in Zstd, Deflate or uncompressed form 🖥️ Snapshot management GUI — browse saved snapshots, inspect their contents, restore earlier data, pin records and export snapshots through an in-game menu 🗺️ Map synchronization — share map data between servers, with configurable sync modes and interaction controls 🔧 Recovery tools — inspect local exception archives and manage data with snapshot import, export and bulk archive commands 🔄 Migration — move existing data over from HuskSync or InvSync with a single command

Install the plugin on every participating Paper or Folia server, point them at a shared Redis service and database, and give each server a unique server-id in server.yml. → Full setup guide on GitHub tip The documentation is still being written. Until the configuration reference lands here, the GitHub README covers installation, configuration files and commands.
Found a bug or have a feature request? Open an issue on GitHub The full source is available under the GPL v3 license — contributions are welcome, translations included

This page groups Sparrow Sync commands by purpose and lists their default permissions. <angle brackets> mark required arguments, and [square brackets] mark optional arguments. Leave out the brackets when entering a command. Use a player name for <player> and the full snapshot UUID for <id>. The commands below use the default configuration. If you change a command or permission in commands.yml, use your configured values instead. Changes to command registration require a server restart.

Command Description Default permission /sparrow-sync status [player] View the plugin's runtime status or a specific player's sync status. sparrow_sync.command.status /sparrow-sync reload Reload the plugin configuration. sparrow_sync.command.reload Without a player name, status shows the server ID, storage type, Redis connection status, tasks, sessions, and other runtime information. With a player name, it shows details such as the player's lock holder and latest snapshot, which can help when investigating sync issues. reload applies settings that support reloading. Settings whose comments specify a restart, as well as command registration itself, require a server restart to take effect.

Command Description Default permission /sparrow-sync snapshot list <player> [page] List a player's snapshots with pagination. sparrow_sync.command.view /sparrow-sync snapshot view <player> <id> Open the details GUI for a snapshot. Players only. sparrow_sync.command.view /sparrow-sync exception list [player] [page] List exception archives saved on this server, optionally filtered by player. sparrow_sync.command.view /sparrow-sync exception view <file> View the report for an exception archive. sparrow_sync.command.view Start with snapshot list to find a snapshot, then open its details to inspect items and other data. Page numbers start at 1; omitting the page shows the first page. Exception archives are stored locally, so exception commands only access files on the current server. For <file>, use the relative path shown in the exception list. Without a player name, exception list 2 displays the second page of all exception archives. If a player name consists entirely of digits, include a page number as well so the name is not interpreted as a page number.

Command Description Default permission /sparrow-sync snapshot capture <player> Immediately create a snapshot for an online player. sparrow_sync.command.capture /sparrow-sync snapshot restore <player> <id> Restore a player's data from a snapshot. sparrow_sync.command.restore /sparrow-sync snapshot pin <id> Pin a snapshot to exclude it from automatic rotation cleanup. sparrow_sync.command.pin /sparrow-sync snapshot unpin <id> Unpin a snapshot so it becomes eligible for automatic rotation cleanup again. sparrow_sync.command.unpin /sparrow-sync snapshot delete <id> Delete a snapshot. sparrow_sync.command.delete /sparrow-sync exception delete <file> Delete a local exception archive and its associated diagnostic files. sparrow_sync.command.exception.delete

capture requires the player to be online, either on the current server or another server participating in synchronization. It captures the player's current data and saves it as a new snapshot. restore supports both online and offline players. For online players, the plugin performs the restore on the server they are playing on. For offline players, the restored data loads on their next login. The snapshot must belong to the specified player. Online restores skip some data Online restores follow synchronization.skip-online-restore-data, which skips health and location by default. See Key Configuration Options for the reasons and configuration details.

Use pin to keep a snapshot for the long term. Pinning prevents automatic cleanup; you can still remove the snapshot explicitly with delete. Exception archives are separate local files and should be removed with exception delete.

Command Description Default permission /sparrow-sync snapshot export <format> <id> Export a single snapshot to a file. sparrow_sync.command.export /sparrow-sync snapshot import <file> Import an exported snapshot into the database. sparrow_sync.command.import /sparrow-sync data dump_all [file] Export database data in bulk to a ZIP file. sparrow_sync.command.dumpall /sparrow-sync data import_all <file> Import data in bulk from a ZIP file. sparrow_sync.command.importall

For snapshot export, <format> accepts BINARY or JSON, producing a .snapshot or .json file respectively. Note the argument order: format first, snapshot ID second. Exported files are stored under plugins/SparrowSync/snapshot/output/. To use snapshot import, place the file in that directory and enter its relative path from there. Importing writes the snapshot to the database. To restore a player's data from it, run snapshot restore after importing. Here is an exported JSON snapshot showing its metadata and the contents saved for each data type:

Bulk operations use plugins/SparrowSync/snapshot/dump/. You can specify a ZIP filename for dump_all; if omitted, the plugin generates a name containing a timestamp. To use import_all, place the ZIP in that directory and enter its relative path. Wait for the console to report the result, then check the imported data.

Command Description Default permission /sparrow-sync data migrate <source> Migrate player data from another plugin. Console or RCON only. sparrow_sync.command.migrate Set <source> to husksync or invsync. The original plugin must remain installed and enabled so Sparrow Sync can read its data. Restrict player access before migrating. Once migration is complete and you have verified the data, stop the server, uninstall the original plugin, then start the server and lift the restrictions. See Data Migration for the full procedure and how to handle failed archives.

Command or permission Purpose Default command permission /sparrow-sync gui <player> Open a player's snapshot list GUI. Players only. sparrow_sync.command.view sparrow_sync.ui.edit Allow item interactions and management actions in the GUI. — gui starts at the player's snapshot list, while snapshot view opens a specific snapshot directly. View permission lets you browse snapshot contents. Grant sparrow_sync.ui.edit when someone also needs to perform actions in the interface.
Each book in the list represents a snapshot. Hover over it to see the capture time, save reason, source server, and full ID, then choose the record you want to open.

After opening a snapshot, use the buttons at the top to switch between data views. The image below shows the saved inventory and equipment: Editing permission includes GUI management actions sparrow_sync.ui.edit controls item interactions as well as deleting, pinning, exporting, restoring, claiming items, and teleporting through the interface. These GUI actions check the editing permission independently; they do not also check each corresponding command permission. Only grant it to people who need to manage player data.

Some options in plugins/SparrowSync/config.yml affect how data is retained across servers, how online rollbacks work, and when snapshots are saved. This page explains those options and the tradeoffs to consider before changing them. Each code block below is a relevant excerpt from the main configuration. Find the corresponding section in your existing file before making changes.

config.yml · Unknown data synchronization: # Discard these data types when this server does not recognize them. # Unlisted types are kept. Restart the server after changing this. discard-unknown-data: - sparrow_sync:attributes - sparrow_sync:enchantment_seed - sparrow_sync:experience - sparrow_sync:flight_status - sparrow_sync:game_mode - sparrow_sync:health - sparrow_sync:hunger - sparrow_sync:location Servers do not always synchronize the same data. If a server disables a data type or does not have the plugin that provides it, Sparrow Sync treats the corresponding snapshot content as unknown data. By default, this data is retained in subsequent snapshots so it can be used again when the player returns to a server that recognizes it. The discard list only applies to unknown types Types listed in discard-unknown-data are discarded when this server cannot recognize them. If synchronization for a type is still enabled on this server, it continues to load and save normally. Adding it to this list does not disable synchronization. Whether to keep or discard data depends on whether it is still needed after the player leaves this server. Keep data that is temporarily unused but will be needed on the original server. Consider discarding data managed independently by each server or taken over by another plugin, so old records no longer travel with the player. Game mode and currency illustrate these two choices.

sparrow_sync:game_mode is included in the default discard list. For example, a survival server and a lobby may manage game modes independently, with game mode synchronization disabled in the lobby. Once the player enters the lobby, the survival server's mode does not need to remain in later snapshots. Discarding it prevents an old record from passing through other servers and eventually returning. To share game modes across servers, enable synchronization.data-types.game-mode on the relevant servers. The discard list only handles types that are not registered locally.
documents.s: Why Game Mode Is Usually Discarded

documents.t: Game modes can often be decided independently, but balances usually need to persist across servers. Even if a server does not use a balance, the player may still need it when returning to a server with an economy. For this reason, sparrow_sync:vault is not in the default discard list. The right choice depends on who manages the currency. Situation What to Do The player is only passing through a server without an economy Keep the currency data so the balance continues to travel with snapshots. Another plugin handles cross-server currency synchronization Disable Sparrow Sync's Vault synchronization and add sparrow_sync:vault to the discard list to stop carrying the old balance. In the second case, newly saved snapshots no longer carry the old currency data, preventing an outdated balance from being loaded if synchronization is enabled again later. Existing historical snapshots are not modified in bulk.
documents.s: Currency Depends on Who Manages It

documents.t: config.yml · Early data loading synchronization: # Load player data early to reduce synchronization lag during login. # Recommended. Try disabling the relevant option if compatibility issues occur. native-async-apply: # Basic player data player-data: true # Advancement progress advancements: true # Statistics statistics: true These options are enabled by default. Before the player has fully joined, Sparrow Sync takes over the server's data loading process, prepares the snapshot, and injects its data into that process. This reduces the lag caused by applying large amounts of data after the player enters the game. player-data controls basic player data, while advancements and statistics control advancement progress and statistics. Keep these enabled under normal circumstances; try disabling the relevant option if login or compatibility issues occur. Spawn event compatibility on Paper 1.21.7+ If another plugin handles spawn locations through the legacy PlayerSpawnLocationEvent, it causes the player object to be created early. Advancements and statistics may then fall back to synchronous loading during login, reducing the benefit of this optimization. Not every method of changing the spawn location triggers this behavior.
documents.s: ⚡ Loading Data Before the Player Joins

documents.t: config.yml · Online rollback synchronization: # Skip these types when restoring snapshots to online players. # Login synchronization is unaffected. An empty list restores all types. skip-online-restore-data: - sparrow_sync:health - sparrow_sync:location This list only affects restoring snapshots to online players, not login synchronization. By default, sparrow_sync:health and sparrow_sync:location are skipped so restoring inventory or other data does not also change the player's health and position. Rolling back health can also change whether a player is alive or dead. Sparrow Sync can write the corresponding health state, but it does not deliberately fire a death event to restore a snapshot. Death events cause other plugins to handle drops, penalties, graves, and more. No single event order works for every plugin during a rollback. Event Order Possible Problem Fire the death event, then roll back Other plugins process items that the rollback should have replaced. Roll back, then fire the death event Newly restored items are taken or deducted by death handling, causing another loss. Keep health in the skip list We recommend skipping health during online rollbacks. Keep sparrow_sync:health in this list unless you have verified how the relevant plugins on your server behave.
documents.s: ❤️ Why Online Rollbacks Skip Health by Default

documents.t: config.yml · Map handling synchronization: map: # Handle cross-server maps. Disabled by default. Restart after changing this. # Enabling this changes map items; uninstalling may not fully restore them. enabled: false # SYNC: synchronize map content. HIDE: prevent use on other servers. synchronization_mode: SYNC Map handling is disabled by default. Sparrow Sync can handle map items that pass through its own save and cross-server loading process, but it cannot cover every way other plugins transfer items. A map item uses a numeric identifier, its map ID, to find the corresponding content. Vanilla normally allocates these IDs starting at 0. Each server manages them independently, so the same ID can refer to entirely different maps on two servers. For example, a global market, cross-server auction house, or plugin backpack may send a map directly to another server, bypassing Sparrow Sync's save and loading process. Its original ID may point to a different map on the destination server, causing it to display the wrong content. Enabling map synchronization alone cannot make these transfers safe. Check how maps move between servers first Before enabling this feature, identify the ways maps can move between your servers and make sure they pass through Sparrow Sync's synchronization process wherever possible. If you cannot ensure this, we recommend leaving map handling disabled. Once you understand how maps are transferred, decide what should happen after a transfer: should players continue viewing the original content, or should maps from other servers simply be prevented from displaying the wrong content? Sparrow Sync provides SYNC and HIDE for these two purposes. To store synchronized maps on the destination server without using vanilla's non-negative numbering range, SYNC allocates map IDs below 0. These negative IDs are local identifiers created by Sparrow Sync to link synchronized map items to their data files. HIDE does not store content from other servers, so it does not need these IDs. Mode Synchronizes Map Content Allocates Negative IDs Purpose SYNC Yes Yes Continue viewing maps after switching servers. HIDE No No Prevent maps from other servers from displaying local map art.

Set synchronization.map.enabled to true and use synchronization.map.synchronization_mode: SYNC to synchronize map content so players can still view it after switching servers. The plugin uses the negative IDs described above to create map data files and point map items to them. This substantially changes how map data is handled. Other plugins may assume map IDs are non-negative or manage map files themselves, so compatibility with every map-related plugin cannot be guaranteed. If you find a conflict, open an issue or contact the author so compatibility can be added. Enabling this feature changes map items and data. Uninstalling Sparrow Sync may not fully restore them. Understand these effects before enabling it.

If you do not need to view map content across servers and only want to prevent maps from other servers from being misused, enable map handling and set the mode to HIDE. It makes maps unusable on other servers without allocating negative IDs or storing their content as SYNC does. This prevents ID collisions from making an external map display local map art that players could then steal or take away. It still depends on the map passing through Sparrow Sync and cannot cover direct trades that bypass the plugin.

config.yml · Unknown advancements synchronization: advancements: # Keep advancements and progress not registered on this server. # Disabling this may lose that progress. Disable only if all registries match. keep-unknown-advancements: true Enabled by default, this preserves advancements and progress that are not registered on the current server. For example, a survival server may add custom advancements through a data pack that is not installed in the lobby. Those advancements cannot be recognized while the player is in the lobby. Keeping unknown advancements lets the player retain that progress when returning to the survival server. Disabling it may lose that progress after the player passes through the lobby and their data is saved. When Can This Be Disabled? Keeping unknown advancements requires an additional scan and data processing. If every participating server always has the same advancement registry, including custom data packs and their updates, you can disable this option to avoid that scanning overhead.

config.yml · World saves synchronization: save-triggers: world-save: # Save snapshots for players in a world when that world is saved. enabled: true Enabled by default, this saves snapshots for players in a world when the server saves that world. The usual default autosave interval is 6000 ticks, or about five minutes at 20 TPS. The actual interval depends on the server's autosave settings and performance.
documents.s: ⏱️ Capturing Player Data During World Saves

documents.t: A world save can trigger data capture for many players at once. Sparrow Sync handles it in this order: The player's owning thread captures data that must be read synchronously. An asynchronous thread captures the remaining data, then encodes and saves the snapshot. Fields May Reflect Different Moments Not every field in the snapshot necessarily comes from the same instant. Players can still move, interact with items, or change other state during asynchronous capture. Some fields may therefore reflect different moments; the snapshot does not represent a completely frozen player state.

We have substantially optimized capture overhead, but at extreme player counts such as 1000, reading all data on a single-threaded Paper server's main thread can still cause a noticeable MSPT spike. Splitting capture balances timely saves, thread requirements, and main-thread load. A Rough Estimate for 1000 Players Our rough estimate for a single-threaded Paper server with 1000 players puts the save-time latency spike at about 80 ms, less than two ticks' worth of time at 20 TPS. This figure is only a reference. Actual overhead varies with hardware, player data size, and other plugins. Other synchronization plugins spread capture load in different ways. Some move all capture to asynchronous threads, facing the risk of data changing while it is read. Others delay saves player by player, so players farther down the queue are captured later as the player count grows. Splitting capture aims to keep the wait short while reducing concentrated work on the main thread.

config.yml · Local logs logging: # Save detailed synchronization logs, including entries not shown in the console. # Keep this enabled. Restart the server after changing it. local-file: true # Days to retain logs. Defaults to two weeks; expired files are removed at startup. retention-days: 14 Local logging is enabled by default, and we recommend keeping it enabled. Data loss and unexpected rollbacks are often intermittent. By the time an administrator receives a report, the player may have switched servers several times, making it difficult to reconstruct what happened. Local logs record: Synchronization conflicts encountered during player synchronization. Lock transitions, including acquiring and releasing distributed locks. Capture and save results, tracing data from capture through persistence. Many details omitted from the console are still written to files, allowing you to follow a complete synchronization sequence by player and time. These logs can be verbose and take up disk space. When a data issue occurs, however, they are often essential to identifying where things went wrong. Missing records cannot be recovered later if logging was disabled. Control Disk Usage with the Retention Period logging.retention-days defaults to 14, keeping the last two weeks of logs. Adjust this value to suit your disk space and troubleshooting needs. At startup, the plugin removes .log and .log.gz files older than the retention period.

Exception snapshots are local archives left for administrators to inspect when saving, importing, or migrating data encounters a problem. An archive may contain complete player data, damaged raw content, or only diagnostic information. Check the cause before deciding what can be recovered.

Run this command on the server where the problem occurred: /sparrow-sync exception list It lists exception snapshots for all players on this server, with pagination. You can also filter by player or use a relative path from the list to inspect an archive: Command Purpose /sparrow-sync exception list [player] [page] List all exception snapshots, or filter by player. /sparrow-sync exception view <file> Inspect an archive's identity information, snapshot body status, and readable data. /sparrow-sync gui <player> Open a player's snapshot list, then switch to exception snapshots. These commands require sparrow_sync.command.view by default. The gui command can only be run by a player. The GUI also reads local exception files; it cannot directly browse another server's exception directory. See Permissions & Commands for action permissions. A listed record does not guarantee recoverable data The list can show the player, time, and source from a separate header file, even if the snapshot body is damaged or was never created. When opening the details, check whether the body exists, whether it can be decoded, and which data remains readable.

Archives are stored under plugins/SparrowSync/snapshot/exception/ in four categories: Subdirectory What triggers it What to check first corrupted/ A pending snapshot cannot be read or its overall format cannot be parsed during startup; a snapshot record cannot be decoded during bulk import. Whether the file is complete or has been modified, and any read or format errors in the console. malformed/ Snapshot encoding fails or data violates storage constraints during saving; an individual data block fails validation, decompression, or NBT parsing during bulk import. The affected data type, encoding error, or database constraint. oversized/ A snapshot exceeds a size limit in the plugin's storage layer or database, such as the database packet size limit. The snapshot size, the size of each data type, and the database error. migration/ Reading, decoding, or converting a player's data from another plugin fails, or the converted snapshot cannot be encoded. The source plugin, failure stage, and original exception in the error report.

During normal saving, data explicitly rejected by the storage layer goes into malformed or oversized, depending on the cause. For example, retrying unchanged data usually will not help if it cannot be encoded or already exceeds the storage size limit. When the database is temporarily unavailable, snapshots are saved to plugins/SparrowSync/snapshot/pending/ for another attempt on the next startup. A successful database write removes the local pending files. Files that cannot be read or decoded move to corrupted; snapshots rejected by storage move to malformed or oversized. If the database remains unavailable, the remaining files stay in pending.

During data import_all, the plugin checks each snapshot's overall format and internal data blocks. If an individual record is faulty, it preserves the original record, writes an error report, and continues with the next record. If the database becomes unavailable or an exception archive cannot be written, the entire import stops. Use the console error to investigate. During data migrate, failures to read, convert, or encode source data go into migration. The report's stage field identifies the failing step: read, decode/convert, or encode. The generated migration ZIP then goes through bulk import, so it can also produce the other three categories. See Data Migration for the procedure. Some errors leave no complete archive If a failure occurs before a complete snapshot exists, or local encoding or disk writes also fail, there may be no usable snapshot body. Problems such as an unreadable ZIP or a failure that stops reading from the source plugin altogether may not produce an archive for a specific player. Keep the console errors and local sync logs in these cases as well.

Files belonging to the same record share a filename prefix. Using example.snapshot as an example: File Contents and purpose example.snapshot The snapshot body. It may be a complete snapshot or damaged raw bytes preserved during bulk import. Reading it determines what is usable. example.snapshot.head A separate binary header containing available player identity, snapshot ID, timestamp, save reason, source server, Minecraft data version, and data size summaries for the list view. It does not contain the full inventory data. example.snapshot.error.txt An error report created for bulk import or migration failures. It includes the category, cause, and available player information. Migration reports also identify the source plugin and failure stage. A stack trace is included when the original exception is available. example.snapshot.source Raw data from the source plugin, saved after a migration failure only when the original bytes are available. It remains in the source plugin's format and cannot be imported directly as a Sparrow Sync snapshot. Not every archive contains all these files. Archives from normal saves and startup retries usually contain a body and .head file, without a separate .error.txt; consult the logs for the cause. If migration fails before conversion completes, there may only be a .head, an .error.txt, and an optional .source, with no .snapshot body. If a header is missing or damaged but the body still provides enough information, the plugin attempts to rebuild the header when reading the exception details. This repairs the information used by the list, not damaged player data.

If a snapshot is only partially damaged, you can still access its readable data through the GUI. A decoding failure in one data type does not necessarily make the inventory, ender chest, or other contents unavailable. As a player on the server holding the archive, run: /sparrow-sync gui <player> Switch to that player's exception snapshot list, open the record, and inspect the inventory, ender chest, and other views. If the item data is intact, you can take items directly from the interface. Check what the player actually lost and return those items promptly, without waiting for every problem in the snapshot to be fixed. Taking items requires editing permission Opening the GUI requires sparrow_sync.command.view. Taking items also requires sparrow_sync.ui.edit. Unreadable data cannot be recovered this way; keep the original exception archive for further investigation.

Keep the archive and review its details, error report, and logs from the same time. Address explicit database connection, account permission, disk space, or file access errors first. For oversized, compare the data size with the database limits. Unlike files in pending, exception archives are not automatically retried at startup. Consider opening an Issue or contacting the author when: Data created during normal gameplay repeatedly fails encoding, decoding, validation, or conversion for an unclear reason. Migration from a supported plugin version repeatedly fails for certain players, or reports incompatible interfaces or fields. Snapshot sizes grow unexpectedly or ordinary player data hits a size limit, and you cannot identify the responsible data type. Data has been lost, rolled back, or become inconsistent, requiring investigation with the archives and sync logs. Even the local exception archive cannot be written, or an unexplained program exception occurs. When reporting, package the record's body, header, error report, and raw attachment together, retaining every file that exists. Also include: The Sparrow Sync version, server type and version, and database type. For migration problems, include the source plugin version. The time of the problem, player name or UUID, and the command or steps involved. The complete console error and local sync logs for the affected player and time period. For migration or bulk import problems, the ZIP used and the processing result shown in the console. Remove sensitive configuration values such as connection passwords before posting a public Issue. If player archives cannot be shared publicly, contact the author to arrange how to provide them. Once the problem is resolved and you have kept any backups you need, use /sparrow-sync exception delete <file> to clean up the record. This deletes the body and its associated header, raw attachment, and error report.

If you want to change the database Sparrow Sync uses, export your data with dump_all, switch the storage configuration, then import the archive with import_all. This also works when switching storage types, such as moving from MySQL to PostgreSQL. Enable the whitelist before migrating Enable the whitelist on all servers in the synchronization group and have online players log out before exporting. A whitelist does not disconnect players who are already online. Keep player access restricted until migration is complete so new saves do not leave the exported data out of date.
documents.s: How do I move data to another database?

documents.t: Keep the current database configuration in place. Choose one server connected to it and run this command in its console: /sparrow-sync data dump_all database-migration.zip Wait for the console to confirm that the export completed. The archive is saved to plugins/SparrowSync/snapshot/dump/database-migration.zip. Keep a copy of it before proceeding.

Stop the servers in the synchronization group. Update the persistent storage type and connection settings in config.yml to point to the new database. See Installing the Plugin for database configuration details. Make the same change on every server in the group: they should all use the new database and matching table or collection prefixes, while keeping their individual server-id values.

Start one server with the new configuration, keeping the whitelist enabled, and check that the database connection succeeds. Place the exported ZIP in that server's plugins/SparrowSync/snapshot/dump/ directory, then run: /sparrow-sync data import_all database-migration.zip Wait for the import result in the console. Import the archive once into the shared database; each server does not need its own import.

After a successful import, check player snapshot lists and log in with a test account to verify that data loads correctly. Once everything looks right, start the remaining servers with the new configuration and lift the access restrictions. Keep the original database and exported ZIP until you have finished checking the migration. If the import reports failures, keep access restricted and investigate the console errors first.

Place the Sparrow Sync .jar file in your server's plugins/ folder, then start the server. The plugin generates its configuration files in plugins/SparrowSync/. The main files and folders are shown below: SparrowSync libs translations commands.yml config.yml server.yml The server shuts down on the first startup The server-id in server.yml is empty by default. On the first startup, the plugin reports the missing server ID in the console and shuts down the server. Before starting the server again, complete both steps below: Set a unique server-id for this server in server.yml. Configure Redis and persistent storage in config.yml and make sure the server can connect to both.

Open plugins/SparrowSync/server.yml and replace the empty server-id string with a unique ID for this server. The following example uses lobby for a lobby server. plugins/SparrowSync/server.yml # Configuration version. Do not edit. ___version___: '1' # A unique ID for this server. Each server taking part in synchronization must use a different value. # Set this before startup. Leaving it blank shuts down the server. # Avoid changing it later. A new ID is treated as a new server and may affect synchronization of existing maps. server-id: 'lobby' server-id identifies this server within the synchronization cluster. It is required and must be different from the IDs of all other participating servers. For example, two survival servers could use survival-1 and survival-2, while a lobby server uses lobby. After copying the plugin configuration to another server, remember to change server-id for the new server. Once the server is in use, avoid changing this ID. A different ID is treated as a new server and may also affect synchronization of existing maps. Save server.yml, then configure the database connections below.

Sparrow Sync requires both Redis and one persistent storage backend. Redis handles cross-server communication, session locks, and snapshot caching. Persistent storage keeps player snapshots long-term. Both must be configured. Prepare these services, then open plugins/SparrowSync/config.yml and edit the existing redis and database sections. The examples below only cover connection settings; do not replace the entire file with them.

config.yml · Redis redis: # Redis host, port, and database number. url: 'redis://localhost:6379/0' # Set a username for ACL authentication; otherwise this can be left empty. username: '' # Redis password. Leave empty if no password is configured. password: '' Replace localhost and the port with your Redis address. /0 selects Redis database 0. Servers in the same synchronization group must connect to the same Redis database with the correct credentials.

Choose a storage type with database.type, then fill in its corresponding connection section. Other sections can keep their default values. Storage database.type Connection Section MySQL MYSQL database.mysql MariaDB MARIADB database.mariadb PostgreSQL POSTGRESQL database.postgresql MongoDB MONGODB database.mongodb The following example uses MySQL. First create a database for snapshots, such as minecraft, and prepare an account with permission to create tables and read and write data in that database. config.yml · MySQL example database: # Choose the persistent storage backend. type: MYSQL mysql: # Set the host, port, and database name, keeping the driver parameters you need. url: 'jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/minecraft?connectTimeout=5000&socketTimeout=10000&characterEncoding=UTF-8' # Replace with your database account and password. username: 'sparrow_sync' password: 'your_database_password' # Use the same table prefix across the synchronization group. table-prefix: 'sparrow_sync_' Servers in the same synchronization group should use the same storage type, connect to the same database, and use the same table prefix. For MongoDB, use the same collection-prefix instead. Each server must still have a different server-id. Once the server ID, Redis, and persistent storage are configured, save the files and start the server again. Check the console to confirm that both Redis and persistent storage connected successfully. If a connection fails, use the error message to check the address, credentials, and database permissions before restarting. See Key Configuration Options for other important synchronization settings and their tradeoffs.
Sparrow Sync supports migrating player data from the following plugins: Plugin Supported Versions InvSync 2.0 and later HuskSync 3.8.7 and later

Choose a server and follow the Installation guide to install and configure Sparrow Sync. Keep the source plugin installed; do not uninstall it yet. Make sure it is enabled and can read its existing data. Enable the whitelist during migration We recommend enabling the whitelist before migration to keep other players from joining. If players continue playing during migration, their in-game data will continue to be saved as new snapshots, which may become their latest records instead of the migrated snapshots. Run the migration command in the server console, choosing husksync or invsync for your source plugin: /sparrow-sync data migrate [husksync/invsync] Wait for the migration results to appear in the console. The plugin first reads the source plugin's data, then imports it into Sparrow Sync. Once migration is complete and you have verified the data, shut down the server and uninstall the original HuskSync or InvSync plugin. Then start the server again, lift the join restrictions, and allow players to connect.

If any records fail to migrate, the console will show the number of skipped or failed records. Keep the files generated during this migration for troubleshooting: Directory Contents plugins/SparrowSync/snapshot/dump/ A ZIP containing migration data exported and converted from the source plugin. Its filename starts with sparrow-sync-migrate-. plugins/SparrowSync/snapshot/exception/migration/ Diagnostic data, available raw player data, and error reports for players whose data failed to migrate. Please package the migration ZIP, the affected players' data, and the error reports together and send them to the plugin author for investigation and a fix. Include the migration results from the console. If migration stops while reading the source plugin's data, a complete migration ZIP may not have been generated yet. In that case, provide any generated error files and the console errors.
